name: Japanese Mythology
framing_note: Shinto is a living religious tradition. These narratives are presented as the tradition's own mythic heritage, with the historical layers (Kojiki 712 CE, Nihon Shoki 720 CE, shrine engi) made visible. Modern state-Sinto and pop-culture readings are labeled separately from the primary texts.

name: Greek Mythology
framing_note: Ancient Greek religion is a historical religion. Its myths are attested in primary literary and material sources; disagreements between authors (Hesiod vs. Orphic vs. local cults) are preserved as variants, not resolved.

name: Norse Mythology
framing_note: The beliefs are pre-Christian (attested archaeologically from the Viking Age); the written sources are Christian-era (1220–1300) and post-hoc. The gap between belief and text is part of what this section presents.

name: Ancient Egyptian Religion
framing_note: Ancient Egyptian religion spanned three millennia. There is no single 'official' version: Heliopolitan, Memphite, and Hermopolitan creation traditions coexisted and are presented in parallel, not merged into a genealogy that never existed.

name: Slavic Mythology
framing_note: Pre-Christian Slavic religion left no native written corpus. Named gods are attested (Vladimir's pantheon, 980 CE; chronicles; ethnography), but the narrative layer is largely scholarly reconstruction (Ivanov–Toporov et al.). Every reconstructed claim is badged as such.
period: attested: 10th–12th c. chronicles · ethnographic record: 18th–20th c.

name: Mesopotamian Mythology
framing_note: Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian, and Assyrian traditions are one layered, continuous religious world. Sumerian names survive inside Akkadian texts; the succession of 'supreme' gods (An → Enlil → Marduk) is presented as political history, not mythic replacement.
